notes.33.24: ꝼri (34.17, 34.32) is read as Frigg and þo (34.30, 36.17) as Thor; both look clipped in the transcription. 35.21a repeats 'that he had seen or heard' from 35.21 inside the sentence that runs on into 35.22, apparently a scribal slip; it is translated as it stands.
notes.1.20: Bragi's stanza (1.29–1.31) is compressed skaldic verse: 'the deep disc of estates' (ꝺiuproðul ǫðla) is a kenning for the land torn away and 'brow-moons' are the oxen's eyes; vinæẏia viðꝛí valroꝼ, rendered 'the wide field-plunder of the meadow-isle', is uncertain.
notes.17.14: hapta guð: hǫpt means 'fetters' or 'captives', and in verse also 'gods', so the title may be 'god of captives' or 'god of the gods'.
notes.36.29: Thor is written 'þo', short for Þórr, at 37.27 and 37.32. 37.22: a rǫst, here 'league', is a measure of distance. 38.8: Mim is Mimir. 38.9 writes 'er' twice. 38.10: 'the wise ones of the rock-wall' (vegbergs vísir) are the dwarves. 38.11: 'the linden' is the shield, made of lime-wood; 'there writhes' (snýz) lacks its subject, Jormungand, who opens the next line, and the refrain 'yet, or what?' is written after it, seemingly out of place.
notes.20.14: 20.24-25: the meaning of Eljudnir is uncertain; Ganglati and Ganglot mean 'slow-goer', male and female; 'Falling Peril' renders fallanda forað. 20.26: gnúpleit, 'drooping-faced', is of uncertain sense. 20.32a: hálfu sterkara, 'stronger by half', may mean twice as strong. 21.25: 'their band' (þeira band) where 'this band' would be expected. 21.29: 'a ver' read as 'nú vera', 'seemed to be'. 22.1: 'ꝼello' read as felldu, 'sank'. 22.5: 'gomspai' read as gómsparri, 'gum-spar', i.e. a gag.
notes.11.4: 11.16 ends with the same words as 11.16a ('Ymir the giant. And when he fell...'); they belong after Gangleri's question at 11.17, so the first is a repetition out of place. lúðr (11.19, 11.21) is a word of disputed sense: a box, ark, hollow trunk or mill-frame. 11.21: 'þat er fyrst of man', rendered 'that is the first I remember'. 12.8, 12.11: brár, 'eyelashes' or 'brows'. 12.10: sveiti is sweat, also used of blood. 12.12: 'hard-tempered' (harðmóðgu) clouds, i.e. storm clouds.
notes.31.21: Thor is written 'þo', short for Þórr, at 32.21, 32.22, 32.26, 32.30, 33.8, 33.18, 33.21 and 33.22. 31.26: 'gresiarn', 'iron wire', is of uncertain sense. 31.31-32.1: Logi means 'flame', Hugi 'thought'. 32.10: Old Age renders elli, the name of the old woman Thor wrestled. 32.25 onward: the giant of the fishing is written ẏmer/ẏmí, the same as the primeval Ymir; elsewhere he is called Hymir. 33.2: Himinhriot, perhaps 'heaven-bellower'. 33.3: the bailing-space (austrúm) is where water is baled out of the boat. 33.14: 'god-strength' renders ásmegin, the strength of the Æsir.
notes.12.27: Nott, Dag, Jord, Mani and Sol mean 'night', 'day', 'earth', 'moon' and 'sun'. 12.32: literally 'in each two dœgr', a dœgr being a half-day of twelve hours. 13.9: 'iron-cool' renders ísarnkol, whose sense is uncertain. 13.11: Sæg is the bucket and Simul the pole it hangs from. 13.21: Managarm means 'moon-hound'. 13.24-13.27 quote a stanza of Voluspa: 'snatcher' renders tjúgari, of uncertain sense, and 'the seats of the powers' are the dwellings of the gods.
notes.27.5: Oku-Thor means 'Driving Thor', Thor with his chariot. 27.15: the manuscript repeats words ('vita megu þat megu þat'); translated once. 27.28: 'companions' (lagsmenn) is written with a stray mark. 28.1: the belt of strength is megingjǫrð; 'divine strength' renders ásmegin. 28.24: 'never would he see himself again' is literal; the sense is that Skrymir would not survive. 29.4: as written, the Æsir 'wished to meet him again in good health'; this is probably ironic, or a negative has dropped out.
notes.38.23: 38.23 ends a stanza begun in the preceding lines; 'leagues' renders rastir. 38.30, 38.29a and 38.29b repeat words of 38.30a-38.31 ('spines', 'and the serpents' heads') and look like marginal or interlinear corrections. Nastrond means 'corpse-strand'. 39.4: the question 'or is there then any earth or sky' is repeated inside Har's answer, apparently by scribal error. 39.8: 'runes' (rúnar) may mean secret lore. 39.11: 'grows black' means Surt's fire dies out. 39.12: Vingnir is uncertain; perhaps a name of Thor. 39.17: Elf-glory (Álfrǫðull) is a name for the sun.
notes.39.20: 39.24: the words 'maðr ǫðrum þessar sǫgur' ('man to another these stories') are written a second time, inside the phrase 'ráða ráðum sínum' ('hold their counsels'); a scribal repetition.
notes.10.27: Vidolf, Vilmeid and Svarthofdi are not identified.
notes.14.5: 14.15: 'hvaða' is read as hvaðan, 'whence'. 14.19-14.21 quote Voluspa: Brimir and Blain seem to be names for Ymir, and 'brimi blóðgu' could also mean 'the bloody surf'; 'host' renders drótt, which may be a slip for dróttin, 'lord'.
notes.19.11: 19.11: the fetter is written gleifni (Gleipnir). 19.13: the wolf-joint (úlfliðr) is the wrist.
notes.29.6: 29.31: a bolt-shot (kolfskot) is the range of a blunt arrow. 30.2: the words 'nt er um þenna leik' repeat the end of 30.1 ('reynt er um þenna leik', 'this game has been decided'), apparently a scribal slip; rendered '- about this game -'. 30.8: the manuscript runs 'mikill' and 'lítill' together; 'little' fits the sense. 30.17: a good carrying-brim means the horn can now be carried without spilling. 31.6: Elli means 'old age'.
notes.9.8: Verse. In prose order: thoughtful men (the subject, 'seggir hyggjandi', stands in the next line) let Svafnir's hall-bark gleam on their backs; it was battered with stones. Svafnir is a name of Odin; the birch-bark roofing of his hall, Valhalla, means shields.
notes.18.15: 'Baleful staves' (feiknstafir) ends a quoted stanza: Baldr's land is the one where the fewest such things lie. The word may mean evil runes or evil deeds.
notes.18.27: The verse lacks its verb: 'er þiaza' has no word such as 'dwelt', supplied in brackets. The first half of the compound 'ski-god' (ǫndur-) stands at the end of the previous line.
notes.25.4: The numeral ꝺccc is read as 800 (d = 500). This line ends a quoted stanza; the wolf is presumably Fenrir.

nodes.text: King Gylfi ruled the lands that are now called Sweden. It is told of him that he
gave a certain wandering woman, as payment for her entertainment, one plough's worth of land in his
kingdom, as much as four oxen could plough up in a day and a night. But this woman was one of the Æsir's
kin. She is named Gefjon. She took four oxen from the north, out of Jötunheim;
and they were the sons of a certain giant and of her. She set them before the plough, and the plough went so wide
and deep that it tore the land loose, and the oxen drew that land out onto the sea and westward, and came
to a halt in a certain sound. There Gefjon set the land down and gave it a name and called it Zealand.
And where the land had been taken up, a lake was left behind. It is
now called Lögrinn in Sweden. And the inlets lie in the lake just as the headlands in Zealand.
So says Bragi the Old: Gefjon drew from Gylfi, glad, the deep disc
of estates, so that steam rose from the running beasts, Denmark's increase. The oxen bore, too,
eight brow-moons, where they went before the wide field-plunder of the meadow-isle, [and] four heads.
There was a man named Gylfi; he was a king and skilled in magic.
He wondered that the Æsir folk were so knowledgeable that all things went according to their
will, and he wondered whether that came from their own nature, or whether the cause of it would be
the divine powers to whom they sacrificed. He set out on his journey to Ásgard, and went in secret, and
took on the likeness of an old man, and so disguised himself. But the Æsir were the wiser in this, that they had
the gift of prophecy, and they saw his journey before he came, and made illusions against him. And
was laid with gilded shields, like a shingled roof. So says Thjodolf of Hvinir, that Valhalla
was thatched with shields: On their backs they let gleam (they were battered with stones) Svafnir's hall-bark,
and from there into Niflhel; that is down in the ninth world. Then Gangleri said: What was he doing
said: What was the beginning, or how did it start, or what was there before? High answers: As it says in Völuspá:
It was early in the ages, when nothing was; there was neither sand nor sea nor cool waves; earth was nowhere found, nor
heaven above; there was the gap of Ginnunga, and grass nowhere. Then Just-as-High said: It was many
ages before the earth was made that Niflheim was made, and in the middle of it lies the spring that
is called Hvergelmir, and from it flow the rivers that are called: Svöl, Gunnthrá, Fjörm, Fimbulthul,
Slíd and Hríd, Sylg and Ylg, Víd, Leiptr; Gjöll is next to the gates of Hel. Then Third said:
First, though, there was that world in the southern region which is called Muspell; it is bright and hot; flaming
and burning it is too, and impassable for those who are foreigners there and have no inherited land there. There is one, Surt
by name, who sits there at the land's end to defend the land. He has a flaming sword, and at the end of the world
into rime, and layer upon layer of rime built up, all the way into Ginnungagap. Then Just-as-High said: Ginnungagap,
was as light as windless air. And when the breath of the heat met the rime, so that it melted
and dripped, then from those living drops there quickened [life], by the power of the one who sent the heat,
and it became the likeness of a man, and he is named Ymir. But the frost-giants call him Aurgelmir, and
from him have come the races of the frost-giants, as it says in the Short Voluspa: "All the seeresses are
from Vidolf, all the wizards from Vilmeid, and the *seiðr*-bearers [practitioners of a kind of magic] from Svarthofdi; all the giants have come from Ymir."
to be a god. He was evil, and all his kinsmen; we call them frost giants. And so it is said that when he slept
he broke into a sweat. Then there grew under his left arm a man and a woman, and one of his feet begot a son with the other,
and from there came the families; they are the frost giants. The old frost giant, him we call Ymir. Then
Gangleri said: Where did Ymir dwell, or on what did he live?
Next it was so, when the rime dripped, that from it came a cow, who was called Audumbla, and four rivers of milk
ran from her teats, and she fed Ymir. Then Gangleri said: On what did the cow feed? Har said:
She licked the rime-stones, which were salty, and the first day that she licked the stones there came out of the stones
by evening a man's hair, the second day a man's head, the third day it was a whole man, who is named
Buri. He was fair of face, big and mighty. He begot a son who is named Bor. He married that
woman who is named Bestla, the daughter of the giant Bolthorn, and they had three sons. One was called Odin, the second
Vili, the third Ve. And it is my belief that this Odin and his brothers must be the rulers of heaven and earth.
We think that he must be called so: so is called the one whom we know to be greatest and most glorious, and well
may you let him be called so. Ymir the giant. And when he fell, then there gushed so much
Then Gangleri said: What then became of their peace, or which were the stronger? Then Har answers: The sons of Bor killed
Ymir the giant. And when he fell, then there gushed so much
blood from his wounds that with it they drowned all the race of frost giants, except that one escaped
away with his household; the giants call him Bergelmir. He went up onto his *lúðr* [ark], he and his wife, and was kept safe
there, and from them are descended the families of frost giants. As it says here: Countless winters before the earth was
shaped, then Bergelmir was born; that is the first I remember, when that wise giant on a *lúðr* was
laid. Then Gangleri says: What did the sons of Bor do then, if you believe that they are gods? Har answers: There is not
little to tell of that. They took Ymir and carried him into the middle of Ginnungagap and made the earth from him,
from his blood the sea and the waters. The earth was made from the flesh and the mountains from the bones; stones and
scree they made from the teeth and molars and from the bones that were broken. Then Jafnhar said: From the blood which from the wounds
ran and flowed freely, from that they made the sea, with which they girded and bound together the earth, and laid
that sea in a ring around it, and most men will think it impossible to get across it.
Then Third said: They also took his skull and made the sky from it and set it up over the earth
with four corners, and under each corner they set a dwarf. They are called thus: Austri, Vestri, Sudri,
Nordri. Then they took the embers and sparks that were flying loose, which had been cast out of Muspellsheim,
and set them in the sky, both above and below, to light up heaven and earth. They gave places to all the fires,
some in the sky; some moved freely under the sky, and yet they gave them a place and shaped
their courses. So it is said in ancient lore that from these the days were distinguished, and the count of years.
So it says in Voluspa: The sun did not know where she had her halls; the moon did not know what strength he
had; the stars did not know where they had their places. So it was before this came to be.
Then Gangleri said: These are great tidings that I now hear. A wondrously great
piece of work that is, and skilfully made. How was the earth arranged? Then Har answers: It is circular,
and around it, outside, lies the deep sea. And along that sea-shore they gave lands for
the races of giants to settle. But further in, on the earth, they made a stronghold all around the world against the hostility
of giants, and for that stronghold they used the eyelashes of Ymir the giant, and called that stronghold Midgard. They took
his brain too and threw it into the air and made the clouds from it. As it says here: From Ymir's flesh
was the earth shaped, and from the sweat the sea, the mountains from the bones, the tree from the hair, and from the skull the sky,
and from his eyelashes the gentle powers made Midgard for the sons of men, and from his brain were
those hard-tempered clouds all shaped. Then Gangleri said: A great thing it seems to me they then brought
came the men who inhabit the world? Then High answers: When they were walking along the sea shore, the sons of Bor
found two trees, and took up the trees and shaped people from them. The first gave breath and life, the second wit
and movement, the third a face, speech and hearing and sight. They gave them clothes and names. The man was called
Ask and the woman Embla, and from them sprang the race of men to whom a dwelling-place was given under
Midgard. Next they made themselves a stronghold in the middle of the world, which is called Ásgard; it is called
Troy. There the gods and their kindred lived, and from there came about many events and dealings,
both on earth and in the sky. There is one place that is called Hlidskjálf, and when Odin sat there in
the high seat, he saw over all worlds and every man's doings, and knew all the things he saw. His wife
was called Frigg, Fjörgvin's daughter, and from their family has come the kindred that we call the race of the Æsir,
and for this reason he may be called All-father, because he is father of all the gods and of men and of all that which by his power
was brought to completion. The Earth was his daughter and his wife. By her he begot the first son,
Narvi was the name of a giant who lived in Jotunheim. He had a daughter who was called Nott. She was black and
dark, as was in her family. She was married first to the man who was called Naglfari; their son was called
Aud. Next she was married to the one who was called Anar; their daughter was called Jord. Last of all her husband was
Delling, and he was of the kin of the Æsir. Their son was Dag; he was bright and fair, after his father's side. Then
the All-father took Nott and Dag her son, and gave them two horses and two chariots, and sent them up into the sky,
so that they should ride around the earth every twenty-four hours. Nott rides first on the
horse that is called Hrimfaxi, and every morning he bedews the earth with the drops from his bit.
The horse that Dag has is called Skinfaxi, and all the sky and the earth are lit from his mane. Then said
Gangleri: 'How does he steer the course of the sun or of the moon?' Har answers: 'A man is named Mundilfari who had
two children. They were so fair and beautiful that he called his son Mani and his daughter Sol, and married
her to the man who was called Glen. But the gods were angered at this arrogance, and took the brother and sister
and set [them] up in the sky; they had Sol drive the horses that drew the chariot of the sun, which the gods
had made to light the worlds from the spark that flew out of Muspellsheim. Those horses
are called thus: Alsvid and Arvak. And under the shoulders of the horses the gods set two bellows to
cool them, and in some lore that is called 'iron-cool'. Mani steers the course of the moon and governs
the new moon and the waning moon. He took two children from the earth, who are called thus: Bil and Hjuki, as they were going from
the well that is called Byrgir and carrying on their shoulders [the bucket] that is called Sæg, and the pole Simul. Vidfinn
is named as their father. These children follow Mani, as can be seen from the earth.' Then said Gangleri:
'The sun goes fast, and almost as if she were afraid; and she would not hasten her course any more even if
she feared her death.' Then Har answers: 'It is not strange that she goes furiously: near
is the one who pursues her, and she has no way out but to run away.' Then said Gangleri: 'Who is it that causes her
this trouble?' Har answers: 'They are two wolves, and the one that goes after her is called Skoll. She fears him, and he
will catch her. And the one that runs ahead of her is called Hati, Hrodvitnir's son, and he means to catch the moon,
and so it will be.' Then said Gangleri: 'What is the wolves' lineage?' Har says: 'A giantess lives east of Midgard,
in the forest that is called Ironwood. In that forest live the troll-women who are called Ironwood-women.
And the old giantess bears many giants as sons, and all in the shapes of wolves, and from there have come
these wolves. And it is said that of that kin one will be the mightiest, who is called Managarm.
He fills himself with the life of all the men who die, and he swallows the moon, and spatters the sky with blood
and all the air. Because of that the sun loses her shine, and the winds are then unquiet and roar from this side
and from that. So it says in Voluspa: "In the east dwells the old one in Ironwood, and gives birth there to
the offspring of Fenrir; of them all one in particular will become the moon's snatcher in a troll's shape. He fills himself
with the life of doomed men, reddens the seats of the powers with red gore; black grows the sunshine in the summers after,
all weathers treacherous. Do you know yet, or what?"
that the gods made a bridge from earth to heaven, which is called Bifrost? You will have seen it;
Asgard?' Har answers: 'In the beginning he set rulers in seats and asked them to decide with
him the destinies of men and to give counsel on the ordering of the stronghold. That was at the place called Idavoll, in the middle of
the stronghold. Their first work was to make the temple in which their twelve seats stand, besides
the high seat that the All-father has. That house is the best built on earth and the largest; it is all, outside and
inside, like pure gold. That place people call Gladsheim. Another hall they made; that was
the sanctuary that the goddesses had, and it was a very fair house; people call it Vingolf. Next they laid
a forge, and for it they made hammer and tongs and anvil, and from these all the other tools; and after that
they worked metal, stone and wood, and so abundantly the metal that is called gold that all their household goods
and all their harness they had of gold; and that age is called the Golden Age, before it was spoiled by the arrival
of the women who came out of Jotunheim.
Next the gods sat down in their seats and set up their courts, and called to mind whence the dwarfs
had quickened, in the soil and down in the earth, like maggots in flesh. The dwarfs
had first taken shape and come to life in the flesh of Ymir, and were maggots then; but by the decree
of the gods they came to have human wit and had the likeness of men; and yet they live in the earth and in stones.
Modsognir was the foremost, and the second Durin. So it says in Voluspa: "Then all the powers went to their judgement-seats, the most holy
gods, and took counsel about this: who should shape the host of dwarfs out of bloody Brimir and out of Blain's
limbs. There many likenesses of men were made, dwarfs in the earth, as Durin said." And these

that root is Hvergelmir, and Nidhogg gnaws the root from beneath. But under that root which faces the frost-giants
there is Mimir's well, in which wisdom and understanding are hidden, and the one who owns the well is called Mimir.
He is full of wisdom because he drinks from the well out of the horn Gjallarhorn.
Urd's Well. There the gods have their place of judgement. Every day the Æsir ride up there over the bridge
Bifrost; it is called that, and also Asbru. The horses of the Æsir are named thus: Sleipnir is the best; Odin owns him; he has eight

to busy themselves with, or what have they done to win renown? High said: Thor is the foremost of them, he who is called
Asa-Thor or Oku-Thor. He is the strongest of all gods and men. He has his realm in the place called Thrudvangar,
he is called Oku-Thor. He also owns three treasures. One is the hammer Mjollnir, which the frost giants

baleful staves. The third of the Æsir is called Njord. He lives in heaven at the place called Noatun. He rules over
can give them wealth in lands and movable goods; he is to be called on for that. Njord is not of the Æsir's kin. He was brought up
in Vanaheim, but the Vanir gave him as a hostage to the gods, and took in exchange as a hostage the one who is called Hoenir. He
became [the pledge of] the settlement between the gods and the Vanir. Njord has the wife who is called Skadi, daughter of the giant Thjazi. Skadi
god or ski-lady. So it is said: Thrymheim it is called, where Thjazi [dwelt], that very mighty giant;
in looks and mighty. Frey is the most renowned of the Æsir. He rules over the rain and the shining of the sun, and with them
the growth of the earth; and it is good to call on him for good harvests and peace. He also rules the prosperity of men. And Freyja
is the most renowned of the goddesses. She has the dwelling in heaven that is called Folkvang, and wherever she
rides to battle, she has half the slain, and Odin half. So it is said here: "Folkvang it is called, and
gods? High said: There is yet a god who is called Tyr. He is the boldest and most courageous, and he has great power over victory in battles.
on his part, that when the Æsir lured the Fenris Wolf into having the fetter Gleipnir laid on him, he did not trust
them to release him until they laid Tyr's hand in his mouth as a pledge. And when the Æsir
would not release him, he bit the hand off at the place now called the wolf-joint; and he is one-handed, and he is not called
a peacemaker of men. One is called Bragi. He is renowned for wisdom, and most for eloquence and skill with words.
called the *bragr* [foremost] of men or *bragr* of women who has more eloquence than others, woman or man. His
wife is Idunn. She keeps in her box the apples which the gods are to bite on when they grow old,

One is called Ull, son of Sif, stepson of Thor. He is so good an archer and so skilled on skis that no one can [compete] with him

There is also counted among the Æsir one whom some call the slanderer of the Æsir and the originator of deceits and the disgrace of all
gods and men. He is named Loki or
Lopt, son of the giant Farbauti. His mother is called Laufey or Nal. His brothers are Byleist
and Helblindi. Loki is handsome and fair in looks, evil in disposition, very changeable in
his ways. He had beyond other men that wisdom which is called cunning, and tricks for every purpose. He brought
their son, Nari or Narvi. Loki had yet more children. Angrboda is the name of a giantess in Jotunheim;
with her Loki begot three children. One was the Fenris Wolf, the second Jormungand, that is the Midgard Serpent,
the third is Hel. And when the gods learned that these three siblings were being brought up in Jotunheim,
and the gods traced through prophecies that from these siblings great misfortune would
befall them, and evil seemed to be expected, first from the mother's side and worse still from the father's,
then Allfather sent the gods to take the children and bring them to him. And when they came to him, he threw
the serpent into the deep sea that lies around all lands, and that serpent grew so that he lies in the middle of
the ocean around all lands and bites on his own tail. Hel he threw into Niflheim and gave her authority over nine worlds,
that she should share out all lodgings among those who were sent to her, and those are men dead of sickness
and dead of old age. She has great dwellings there, and her walls are exceedingly high and her gates huge.
Eljudnir is the name of her hall, Hunger her dish, Famine her knife, Ganglati [her] thrall, Ganglot
[her] bondmaid, Falling Peril [her] threshold. She is half black-blue and half flesh-coloured;
by this she is easily known, and rather drooping-faced and grim-looking.
The Æsir brought up the wolf at home, and Tyr alone had the courage to go up to him and give him food.
And when the gods saw how much he grew each day, and all prophecies said that he was destined
to harm them, the Æsir adopted this plan: they made a very strong fetter, which they called Læding, and
carried it to the wolf and bade him try his strength against the fetter. And it did not seem to the wolf too much for him,

But the beginning of this tale is that Oku-Thor set out with his goats and chariot, and with him the god
who is called Loki. They come in the evening to a farmer and get lodging for the night there. And in the evening
Thor took his goats and slaughtered both; after that they were skinned and carried to the cauldron. And when it was cooked, Thor sat down

was called Thjalfi, and the daughter Roskva. Then Thor laid the goatskins further out from the fire and said that the farmer
and his household should throw the bones onto the goatskins. Thjalfi, the farmer's son, took hold of
the goat's thigh-bone and split it with his knife and broke it open for the marrow. Thor stayed there for the night,
and in the small hours before day he got up and dressed, took the hammer Mjollnir, raised it and hallowed the goatskins.
Then the goats stood up; one of them was lame in the hind leg. Thor saw that and declared that the farmer
or his household could not have dealt sensibly with the goat's bones; he perceives that it was broken,
the thigh-bone. There is no need to make a long story of it; all may know how frightened the farmer
must have been when he saw that Thor let his brows sink down over his eyes; and as for what he saw of the eyes, he thought he would
fall down at the sight of them alone. He clenched his hands on the hammer-shaft so that they went white,
the knuckles. And the farmer did as was to be expected, and all the household cried out loudly, begged for mercy, offered
as atonement all that they owned. And when he saw their terror, his rage left him and he calmed down, and
took from them in settlement their children, Thjalfi and Roskva, and they then became his bound servants, and they have followed
him ever since. He left the goats behind there and began the journey east into Jotunheim, and
[went] all the way to the sea, and then he went out over the sea, the deep one; and when he came to land, he went ashore, and
with him Loki, Thjalfi and Roskva. When they had walked a little while, a great forest lay before them.
They walked all that day until dark. Thjalfi was the fastest of foot of all men; he carried Thor's bag,
but provisions were not good to come by. When it had grown dark they looked for a place for the night, and found before them a hall,
a very large one; there was a doorway at the end, as wide as the hall. There they looked for a night's lodging.
But in the middle of the night there was a great earthquake; the earth heaved under them in jolts, and there shook
the house. Then Thor stood up and called to his companions, and they searched about and found a side-room on the right hand,
in the middle of the hall, and went in there. Thor sat down in the doorway, and the others were further in, behind him,
and they were afraid. But Thor held the hammer-shaft and meant to defend himself. Then they heard
a great groaning and roaring. And when it came towards dawn, Thor went out and sees a man lying a short way from
him in the forest, and he was not small. He was asleep and snoring mightily. Then Thor thought he understood what noises
there had been in the night. He buckled on his belt of strength, and his divine strength grew. But at that
moment the man wakes, stood up quickly; and then it is said that for once Thor lost his nerve to strike him with
the hammer, and he asked him his name. He named himself Skrymir. 'But I do not need,' he says, 'to ask you
your name; I know that you are Asa-Thor. But have you dragged off my glove?' He reached
out and picked up the glove. Thor sees then that he had had it for a hall in the night, and
the side-room was the thumb of the glove. Skrymir asked whether Thor wanted to have his company, and Thor
agreed to that. Then Skrymir took and untied his provision-bag and got ready to eat his morning meal, and Thor in another place

Skrymir falls asleep and snored hard, and Thor took the provision-bag and is about to untie it. But it must be told, unbelievable as

looser than before. And when he sees that this labour comes to nothing, he becomes angry and gripped the hammer Mjollnir

for bed. Thor said that they were going to sleep then. They then go under another oak. It is the truth,
to tell you, that it was not then free of fear to sleep. And at midnight Thor hears that Skrymir

But Skrymir sat up and stroked his cheek and said: 'Can there be some birds sitting in
the tree above me? I suspected, when I woke, that some litter from the branches fell on my head.

way ahead to the stronghold that is called Utgard. I have heard that you have whispered among
yourselves that I was no small man in stature; but you will see bigger men there if you come into Utgard.

did not have the goats, nor any companions. He went out from Asgard in the likeness of a young lad, and came one

come from him, since he was small and only a youngster: and you will get cold if I sit as long and as far out as I

would at once let the hammer crash down on him. But he let it pass, because he meant then to test
his strength in another place. He asked Ymir what they should have for bait, but Ymir told him
to get bait for himself. Then Thor turned away to where he saw a certain herd of oxen that Ymir
owned. He took the biggest ox, which is called Himinhriot, and tore off its head and went with it to the sea.

and rowed, and Ymir thought there was good speed from his rowing. Ymir rowed forward in the bow, and swiftly went

fish. But Thor says he wants to row much further, and they took another spurt of rowing. Then Ymir said

with his hand. The Midgard Serpent gaped over the ox-head, and the hook stuck in the serpent's gum.

and all were of one mind toward him who had done the deed. But no one could take vengeance; it was so great a place of sanctuary there.
And when the Æsir came to their senses, the first thing was that weeping broke out, so that no one could tell another
in words of his grief. But Odin bore this loss the worst, in that he had the greatest
understanding of how great a loss and bereavement for the Æsir lay in Baldr's death. And when the gods came to their senses,
then Frigg spoke and asked who there was among the Æsir who wished to win all my love and favour, and was willing
to ride the road to Hel and try whether he could find Baldr, and offer Hel a ransom, if she will let
Baldr go home to Ásgard. And he is named Hermod the Bold, Odin's son, who for that
errand came forward. Then Sleipnir, Odin's horse, was taken and led out, and Hermod mounted that horse
and galloped away. And the Æsir took Baldr's body and carried it to the sea. Hringhorni was the name of the ship
of Baldr. It was the greatest of all ships. The gods wanted to launch it and hold Baldr's burning on it, but
the ship would not move at all. Then [word] was sent to Jötunheim for the giantess who is named Hyrrokkin.
And when she came, riding a wolf, with a viper for reins, she leapt off the steed, and Odin
called four berserks to tend the steed, and they could not hold it unless they felled
it. Then Hyrrokkin went to the prow of the vessel and pushed it out at the first thrust, so that fire
flew from the rollers and all lands shook. Then Thor grew angry and gripped the hammer and would then
have broken her head, but all the gods asked peace for her. Then Baldr's body was carried out onto the ship. And
when his wife Nanna, Nep's daughter, saw that, she burst with grief and died. She was carried onto the pyre and it was set
on fire. Then Thor stood by and hallowed the pyre with Mjöllnir. And in front of his feet ran a certain dwarf
who is named Litr. And Thor kicked him with his foot and pushed him into the fire, and he burned.
To this burning came many kinds of folk. First to tell of Odin: with him went Frigg and the valkyries
and his ravens. And Freyr drove in a chariot with the boar that is called Gullinbursti or Slídrugtanni. And
Heimdall rode the horse that was called Gulltopp, and Freyja [drove] her cats. There came also a great host
of frost-giants and mountain-giants. Odin laid on the pyre the gold ring that is called Draupnir. It afterwards had
this property, that every ninth night eight rings of equal weight dripped from it. The horse
of Baldr was led onto the pyre with all its harness. And this is to be told of Hermod, that he rode nine nights through dark
and deep valleys, so that he saw nothing until he came to the river Gjöll and rode onto the Gjöll bridge.
It is roofed with gleaming gold. Módgud is the name of the maiden who guards the bridge. She asked him his name
and his kin, and said that the day before five troops of dead men had ridden over the bridge, but the bridge resounds no
less under you alone, and you do not have the colour of dead men. Why do you ride here on the road to Hel? He said: I am to ride
to Hel to seek Baldr. Or have you seen anything of Baldr on the road to Hel? She said that Baldr had
ridden over the Gjöll bridge there, but down and to the north lies the road to Hel. Then Hermod rode on until he came
to the gates of Hel. Then he got off the horse and girthed it tight, mounted and spurred it, and the horse
leapt so hard over the gate that it came nowhere near it. Then he rode up to the hall and got down from the horse's back,
went into the hall, and saw his brother Baldr sitting there in the high seat; and Hermod stayed there for the night.
In the morning he asked Hel that Baldr should ride home with him, and told how great
a weeping there was among the Æsir. But Hel said that it should be tested in this way whether Baldr was as much loved as was said: and
if all things in the world, living and dead, weep for him, then he shall go back to the Æsir, but stay with Hel
if any speaks against it or will not weep. Then Hermod stood up, and Baldr led him out of the hall
and took the ring Draupnir and sent it to Odin as a keepsake. And Nanna sent Frigg a linen cloth and still more
gifts, [and] to Fulla a gold finger-ring. Then Hermod rode back his way and came to Ásgard and told all the news
that he had seen or heard.
Next the Æsir sent over the whole world that he had seen or heard.
messengers to ask that Baldr be wept out of Hel. And all did so: the men and the living creatures
and the earth and the stones and trees and every metal, just as you will have seen that these things weep
when they come out of frost into warmth. When the messengers were going home and had carried out their errand well,
they find in a certain cave where a giantess sat. She called herself Thökk. They ask her to weep Baldr
out of Hel. She said this: Thökk will weep dry tears at Baldr's burning. Living or dead,
I had no good of the old man's son. Let Hel keep what she has. And people guess that this was Loki, Laufey's
son, who has done the most evil among the Æsir. Then Gangleri said: A very great deal did Loki bring about, when he caused first
that Baldr was slain, and also that he was not set free from Hel. Or was any of this
avenged on him? High said: He was paid back for it in such a way that he will feel it for a long time.
When the gods had become as angry with him as was to be expected, he ran away and hid himself on a certain mountain,
built a house there with four doors, so that he could see out of the house in all directions. And often by day
he changed himself into the likeness of a salmon and hid then in the place called Fránangr Falls. He considered what
device the Æsir might find to catch him in the falls. And once when he sat in the house he took linen yarn
and knotted it into meshes, as nets have been made since, and a fire burned in front of him. Then he saw that the Æsir were a short way from
him, and Odin had seen from Hlidskjálf where he was. He at once ran out into the river, and threw
the net onto the fire. And when the Æsir come there, the one who went in first was he who was wisest of all, who
is named Kvasir, and when he saw in the fire the ash where the net had burned, he understood that it
must be a device for catching fish, and told the Æsir. Next they set to and made themselves a net
on the pattern of what they saw in the ash that Loki had made. And when the net was ready, the Æsir go to the river
and cast the net into the falls. Thor held one end of the net, and all the Æsir held the other, and they drew
the net. But Loki went ahead of it and lay down between two stones. They drew the net over him
and felt that something living was in the way. And they go a second time up to the falls and cast out the net, and tie on
something so heavy that nothing could pass beneath. Then Loki goes ahead of the net, and when he sees that it was a short way
to the sea, he leaps up over the net-rope and swims up into the falls. Now the Æsir saw where he went;
they go up again to the falls and divide the company into two groups, and Thor then wades along the middle of the river,
and so they go out toward the sea. And when Loki sees two choices: it was mortal danger to leap into the sea,
and the other was to try again over the net; and that he did: he leapt as quickly as he could over the net-rope.
Thor grabbed after him and caught hold of him, and he slipped in his hand, so that the hand stopped
at the tail. And for that reason the salmon has been narrow toward the tail ever since.
Now Loki was taken, without quarter, and brought into a certain cave. Then they took three slabs of rock
and set them on edge and struck a hole in each slab. Then Loki's sons were taken, Váli and Nari
or Narfi. The Æsir changed Váli into the likeness of a wolf, and he tore apart his brother Narfi. Then
the Æsir took his guts and bound Loki with them over the three edges. One stands under his shoulders, the second
under his loins, the third under the backs of his knees. And those bonds turned to iron. Then Skadi took a venomous snake
and fastened it up over him, so that the poison would drip from the snake into his face. But Sigyn,
his wife, sits beside him and holds a basin under the drops of poison. And when the basin
is full, she goes and pours away the poison. But meanwhile the poison drips into his face. Then
he jerks so hard against it that the whole earth shakes; that is what you call earthquakes. There he lies in bonds until
Ragnarök. Then Gangleri said:
Ragnarok? Of that I have never heard tell before. Har said: There are great tidings of it
to tell, and many. The first of them is that there comes a winter which is called Fimbulwinter.
Then snow drives from all quarters; the frosts are great then, and the winds sharp; there is no use
of the sun. Those winters come three together, with no summer between. But before that, three other winters pass in such a way
that there are then great battles throughout the world. Then brothers kill each other for greed's sake, and no one
spares father or son in manslaughter or in the breaking of kinship. So it says in Voluspa: Brothers will fight
and be each other's slayers; sisters' sons will defile kinship. It is hard among men, great adultery;
an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cloven; a wind-age, a wolf-age, before the world plunges down. Then that happens
which will seem great tidings: the wolf swallows the sun, and people think that a great harm. Then the
other wolf takes the moon, and he too does great damage. The stars then vanish from the sky. Then there is also
this among the tidings, that the whole earth and the mountains shake so that trees are torn up out of the earth and the mountains crash down,
and all fetters and bonds break and snap. Then the Fenris Wolf gets loose. Then the sea surges over
the lands, because the Midgard Serpent then writhes in giant-fury and makes its way up onto the land. Then this also happens, that
Naglfar comes loose, the ship that is so called. It is made of dead men's nails, and for that reason it is worth
a warning: if a man dies with uncut nails, that man adds much material to the ship Naglfar,
which gods and men would want finished late. And in this flood of the sea Naglfar floats. Hrym
is the name of the giant who steers Naglfar. And the Fenris Wolf goes with gaping mouth, and the lower
jaw is on the earth and the upper against the sky; he would gape wider if there were room for it. Flames
burn from his eyes and nostrils. The Midgard Serpent blows so much poison that he spatters all the air and the sea,
and he is most terrible, and he is at the wolf's other side. In this din the sky splits open, and there ride
from it the sons of Muspell. Surt rides first, and before and after him [is] burning fire. His sword is
very good; from it shines a light brighter than from the sun. And when they ride over Bifrost, it breaks,
as was said before. The sons of Muspell press forward onto the field which is called Vigrid. There come also
the Fenris Wolf and the Midgard Serpent. There too by then have come Loki and Hrym, and with him all the frost giants,
and all Hel's company follow Loki. And the sons of Muspell have a battle-line of their own, and it is very bright.
The field Vigrid is a hundred leagues wide each way. And when these things
come to pass, Heimdall stands up and blows mightily on the Gjallarhorn and wakes up all the gods, and
they hold an assembly together. Then Odin rides to Mimir's well and takes counsel from Mimir for himself and his host.
Then the ash Yggdrasil shakes, and nothing then is without fear in heaven or on earth. The Æsir arm
themselves, and all the *einherjar* [Odin's chosen champions], and they press forward onto the field. Odin rides first, with a golden helmet and a fair
mail-coat and his spear, which is called Gungnir; he makes for the Fenris Wolf. And Thor [goes] forward at the other
side of him, and he cannot help him, because he has his hands full fighting the Midgard Serpent. Frey
fights against Surt, and there is a hard clash before Frey falls. That becomes his death, that he lacks
that good sword which he gave to Skirnir. Then the dog Garm has also got loose, who is bound
before Gnipahellir. He is the greatest of monsters. He has a fight with Tyr, and each becomes the other's
bane. Thor wins the fame of slaying the Midgard Serpent, and steps away from there nine paces; then he falls
dead to the earth from the poison that the serpent blew on him. The wolf swallows Odin; that becomes his
death. But straight after, Vidar strides forward and steps with one foot into the wolf's lower jaw. On
that foot he has the shoe that has been gathered together through all time: those are the scraps that people cut
from their shoes at toe or heel. Therefore those scraps should be thrown away by the man who means to take care
to come to the help of the Æsir. With one hand he takes the wolf's upper jaw and tears apart its maw,
and that becomes the wolf's death. Loki has a battle with Heimdall, and each becomes the other's slayer. Next
Surt flings fire over the earth and burns the whole world. So it says in Voluspa: Loud blows
Heimdall, the horn is aloft; Odin speaks with Mim's head. Yggdrasil's ash trembles where it stands,
the old tree groans, and the giant gets loose. What is with the Æsir? What is with the elves?
All Jotunheim roars, the Æsir are at assembly; the dwarves groan before their stone doors, the wise ones of the rock-wall. Do you know
yet, or what? Hrym drives from the east, the linden is lifted before [him]; there writhes, yet, or what?
gods; a hundred leagues it is every way; that field is marked out for them.' Then said Gangleri: 'What will
be left then, when the whole world is burned, and all the gods are dead, and all the *einherjar* [Odin's chosen dead warriors] and all mankind? And
you have said before that every man shall live in some world through all ages.' Then Third answered:
'Many dwellings there are then, good ones, and many evil. Best then is to be in heaven; and very good
it is for good drink, for those who take pleasure in that, in the hall that is called Brimir; it stands on Okolnir.
There is also a good hall that stands on Nidafjoll, made of red gold; it is called Sindri. In these
halls shall good and virtuous men dwell.

On Nastrond there is a great hall, and an evil one, and its doors face north. It is all woven of serpents' spines,
and the serpents' heads
all face into the house and blow poison, so that along the hall run rivers of poison, and wading those
rivers are oath-breakers and murderers, as it says here: "A hall I know standing far from the sun, on Nastrond;
its doors face north; drops of poison fall in through the roof-vent; that hall is woven of serpents' spines.
There shall wade heavy streams perjured men and murderers." But in Hvergelmir it is
worst: there Nidhogg torments the corpses of the dead.' Then said Gangleri: 'Do any of the gods live then,
or is there then any earth or sky?' Har said: 'Up shoots the earth then - or is there then any earth or sky -
out of the sea, and it is then green and fair; the fields grow then unsown. Vidar and Vali live, so that neither
the sea nor Surt's fire has harmed them, and they dwell on Idavoll, where Asgard was before;
and there then come the sons of Thor, Modi and Magni, and they have Mjollnir there. Next there come
Baldr and Hod from Hel. They all sit down together then and talk, and recall their runes, and
speak of all the events that had happened before, of the Midgard Serpent and of the Fenris Wolf. Then
they find there in the grass the golden gaming-pieces that the Æsir had owned. So it is said: "Vidar and Vali
will dwell in the sanctuaries of the gods when Surt's fire grows black; Modi and Magni shall have Mjollnir
of Vingnir at the battle's end." And at the place called Hoddmimir's Holt two people hide during Surt's
fire, who are called thus: Lif and Leifthrasir, and they have the morning dews for food. And from these people
comes so great a progeny that the whole world is peopled. As it says here: "Lif and Leifthrasir, and
they will hide in the holt of Hoddmimir; the morning dews they will have for food, and from them
the generations of men will be born." And this will seem strange to you: that the sun has borne a daughter no less fair
than she is, and she will then go her mother's paths, as it says here: "One daughter Elf-glory bears, before her
Fenrir destroys; she shall ride, when the powers die, the maid, her mother's roads." But now, if you can [go] further
tell further of the course of the world; and make use now of what you have learned.' Next Gangleri heard
a great din on every side of him, and he looked out to his side; and when he looks about further, he stands
outside on a level plain. He then goes away on his way, and
comes home into his kingdom and tells the tidings that he has seen or heard; and after him each
man told another these stories. But the Æsir then sit down to talk and hold - man to another these stories -
their counsels, and call to mind all this account that was told here, and give these names,
the same that were named before, to the men and places that were there, so that when long
ages had passed, people should not doubt that they were all one, those Æsir of whom it was now told
and these to whom the same names were given. There, then, Thor was named, and that is Asa-Thor,
the old Thor. He is Oku-Thor, and to him are ascribed the great deeds that Hector did
in Troy. And people believe that the Turks told of Ulysses, and that they called him
Loki, because the Turks were his greatest enemies.
